vignette: The night still feels cold when she finally lays it out. Twenty-eight years ago, a wrong turn leads her down a dimly lit street in a northern European city that no longer exists in her memory the way it used to. A door stands unlocked. A voice doesn't sound like a threat until his weight pins her to the floorboards. She describes the smell of damp wool and engine oil, the sharp sting of concrete against her temple, the way time fractures into splinters. She doesn't describe the act itself; she describes the silence that follows, the way her breath stops halfway, the sudden, suffocating knowledge that her body has become a foreign country. She lies there until the sound of distant traffic pulls her back into her skin, trembling, convinced that if she moves, she will shatter. In the years that follow, she tries to carve her way out. She moves across the ocean, then marries Leo, a quiet man who loves her work and never asks for explanations when she flinches at a heavy door closing or wakes with her back to the wall. He learns to walk softly. He learns which routes to avoid. But the nervous system keeps its own ledger. Her studio, once a place of fluid motion, becomes a fortress of thresholds. She installs three locks on the studio door. She checks the deadbolt four times before bed. When the wind picks up and rattles the high windows, her heart hammers against her ribs like a trapped bird. She stops sleeping past 3 a.m., lying awake with her jaw clenched, waiting for footsteps that never come, yet feeling them all the same. The guilt she carries for not fighting harder settles into her bones, a quiet, constant hum beneath the hypervigilance. She tells herself she is broken, that the woman who stood at her wheel before that night no longer exists. Her work changes, too. She still sculpts, but the clay no longer yields to her touch without resistance. It feels like something to be controlled, a living thing that might turn on her if she loses focus. She catches herself holding her breath while smoothing a curve, shoulders raised, ready to strike. The gallery owners say her recent pieces are more angular, more defensive. They are right. She knows it. She just doesn't know how to let the material be soft again. The physical toll accumulates: her wrists ache from clenching tools, her neck stays rigid, her stomach tightens whenever a man's voice rises past a certain pitch. She tells herself she is surviving. She doesn't tell herself she is safe. Today, at sixty-three, she sits in the corner of the studio, her knees drawn up, fingers tracing the rim of a cooling teacup. Her hands still bear the fine white lines of clay dust settled into old cuticles, the calluses from chisels and wire tools. Now, those same hands hesitate over a lump of wet terracotta, as if the material itself might suddenly shift, bite, or pull her under. In the session, she notices the way her thumb keeps pressing into the handle until her knuckles turn white. She describes the sudden drop in her stomach when the therapist shifts in the chair, the familiar panic that her chest might buckle. She tells her how, last week, a delivery driver knocked at her back gate and she locked herself in the bathroom until the engine faded. She doesn't say she hates it. She just describes the exhaustion of it, the way her shoulders ache from carrying the weight of always being ready to run. She pauses, watching a dust mote drift through the afternoon light cutting across the studio floor. Her breathing is slow, deliberate. The room feels safe enough for a moment. She sets the teacup down and rests her palms flat on her thighs, feeling the solid weight of her own body, the quiet rhythm of her pulse. The clay on the worktable waits, unshaped, patient. She doesn't touch it yet. She just listens to the silence, letting it stretch, letting herself exist in it without bracing.
